name: Set of six dining chairs
description: A set of six English Regency dining chairs from the early nineteenth century, with rattan seats and backs set within finely proportioned wooden frames. The design reflects the Regency period’s interest in refined construction, lightness and decorative restraint, as well as the wider fascination with Asian-inspired furniture forms in early nineteenth-century Britain. The Chatsworth Estate in Derbyshire is one of England’s most historically significant country houses and has long been the seat of the Dukes of Devonshire. A Chatsworth Estate label indicates that the chairs were likely part of the furnishings of the house or one of its associated interiors. The provenance connects the set to one of Britain’s most important collecting families, whose holdings have included furniture, works of art and decorative objects assembled over several centuries. Labelled "Chatsworth Estate" on the underside

name: A set of five model 3238 ‘Spanish’ dining chairs and two armchairs designed by Borge Mogensen for Fredericia Stolefabrik Denmark, 1950s
Set of six dining chairs 'Model 465' designed by Helge Sibast & Børge Rammeskov for Sibast Møbler
description: These 'Model 465' dining chairs by Helge Sibast and Børge Rammeskov for Sibast Møbler represent a refined expression of Danish modern design. Crafted in rosewood, the frames display a rich, expressive grain that enhances the sculptural quality of the design, while the upholstered seats in blue wool introduce a soft contrast in both colour and texture. The defining feature of the model is its distinctive “floating” backrest. A gently curved horizontal rail is elevated by slender vertical supports, accented with subtle metal fittings. This construction allows the backrest to appear almost detached from the frame, giving the chairs an open and architectural character. Helge Sibast (1908–1985) was a central figure in Denmark’s mid-century design movement, known for his precise joinery and refined approach to wood construction. Trained as a cabinetmaker in his father’s workshop, he brought a deep understanding of material and technique to his designs. Together with Børge Rammeskov, he developed furniture that combined traditional craftsmanship with modern clarity.

name: An Art Nouveau armchair
Easy chair Designed by Otto Schulz for Boet
description: This vintage furniture armchair is an elegant example of Otto Schulz’s sophisticated Swedish design language. Drawing on the classical Greek klismos and his own “Sulla” model, Schulz developed a generous, sculptural seat with a sweeping back that curves gently around the sitter. By dispensing with a loose seat cushion and instead shaping one deep, integrated seat, he achieved a remarkably pure and modern silhouette that stands out among vintage furniture pieces. Otto Schulz, founder of the influential firm and magazine Boet, was central to Nordic interior culture, and today this rare easy chair sits comfortably alongside the most sought-after Danish vintage design furniture within the broader Scandinavian modern canon.

name: A set of six armchairs 'Model 350' designed by Peter Hvidt and Orla Mølgaard-Nielsen for Søborg Møbler
description: These 'Model 350' armchairs were designed by Peter Hvidt and Orla Mølgaard-Nielsen for Søborg Møbelfabrik and presented publicly at the Cabinetmakers’ Guild Exhibition in 1958. The chairs are constructed in teak, with a clearly articulated, architectural frame defined by straight lines, sharp angles and precise joinery. This structural clarity is balanced by seats and backrests woven in cane with a diagonal herringbone pattern. Peter Hvidt and Orla Mølgaard-Nielsen were key contributors to Danish modern furniture in the post-war period. Through their long-standing collaboration, they developed designs characterised by simplicity and a deep understanding of materials, often bridging traditional cabinetmaking with modern production techniques. Søborg Møbelfabrik played an important role in realising and disseminating their work, becoming one of the manufacturers most closely associated with the international success of Danish modern design during the 1950s and 1960s.

name: Armchair by Niels Jensen
description: This armchair by master cabinetmaker Niels Jensen is crafted in mahogany with a hand-woven cane seat, distinguished by a back panel featuring a finely judged circular cut-out. Each joint is clearly articulated, giving the chair a sense of structure and balance that reflects a disciplined approach rooted in traditional cabinetmaking. The chair type is often referred to as a “Chinese Chair,” reflecting a modern Danish reinterpretation of traditional Ming Dynasty seating, specifically the round-back yuanyi . Characterised by its horseshoe-shaped crest rail, the original form was regarded as a seat of honour in 17th-century China, reserved for high-ranking officials and often upholstered in fine textiles. Niels Jensen is a sixth-generation cabinetmaker of Danish origin whose work is grounded in classical woodworking principles. Over a career spanning nearly four decades, he has built a reputation for producing custom, hand-crafted furniture of consistently high quality. Based in Quebec, Canada, Jensen often works with carefully selected woods, including locally sourced and reclaimed materials, bringing a deep respect for material integrity to each piece.

name: Teak armchair designed by Eva & Nils Koppel for Slagelse Møbelværk
description: This armchair by Eva and Nils Koppel, produced by Slagelse Møbelværk in the 1950s, represents a high point in the couple’s short but significant furniture design period and an important contribution to early Danish modernism. Executed in teak with a seat and back upholstered in patinated brown leather, the chair is defined by its flowing lines and the distinctive, blade-like armrests echoing their famous Model 190 'Medallion' chair. Eva and Nils Koppel were a Danish architect couple who played an influential role in shaping mid century Scandinavian design. After meeting during their studies, they joined the studio of Alvar Aalto in the late 1930s, where his organic modernist principles left a lasting impression on their work. Returning to Denmark, they established their own practice in 1946, which later became one of the country’s most prominent architectural firms, known for major public and residential projects.

name: Folding chair designed by Poul Hundevad
description: This elegant folding chair by Poul Hundevad is a refined example of Scandinavian vintage design from the 1950s. Crafted in Denmark, the chair combines a sculptural patinated oak frame with a floating seat and back in naturally aged leather, creating a warm dialogue between material, form and function. The gently curved legs intersect in a characteristic X-shape, giving the vintage furniture chair both stability and a distinctive architectural profile. Hundevad’s work is closely associated with classic Danish design, where practicality and beauty are inseparable. The chair folds with ease, yet when opened it reads as a fully fledged lounge chair rather than a temporary solution, which places it in the realm of exclusive design furniture rather than simple utility. The rich patina of the oak and leather speaks to decades of careful use and is highly prized among collectors of Scandinavian furniture. This piece offers an authentic expression of Scandinavian vintage design, embodying the craftsmanship, clarity of line and quiet luxury that define the period.

name: Chaise lounge designed by Bruno Mathsson
description: This reclining chaise lounge, model 36 by Bruno Mathsson, is a quintessential example of Swedish modernism and Scandinavian design. Designed with Mathsson’s characteristic focus on ergonomics, the beech frame is elegantly bent into a continuous, flowing line that follows the natural contours of the body. The seat and back are woven in black natural flax webbing, creating a flexible yet supportive surface that gently yields to the sitter. A removable neck pillow in soft grey wool adds an extra layer of comfort and refined tactility. Branded Bruno Mathsson Design, Made in Sweden , this vintage chaise embodies the lightness and clarity that define Scandinavian vintage design. The combination of pale beech, dark webbing, and minimal hardware results in a piece that feels both graphic and warm. Stamped

name: Daybed designed by Ib Kofod-Larsen
description: The daybed reflects Ib Kofod-Larsen’s approach to functional furniture developed during the post-war period in Denmark. The design combines a solid walnut frame with a cane sleeping surface, allowing the piece to function both as seating and as a bed. The frame is constructed with slim proportions and tapered legs, typical of Scandinavian furniture from the period, and emphasises visual lightness and efficient use of material. His work shares formal characteristics with other Danish designers of the time, including organic lines, balanced proportions, and an emphasis on wood as a primary material. Ib Kofod-Larsen was trained as a cabinetmaker and architect, and his work is characterised by attention to proportion, comfort, and craftsmanship. This daybed is representative of his furniture from the period, combining practical construction with a restrained design approach typical of Danish modern furniture of the mid-20th century.

name: Pair of easy chairs designed by Frits Schlegel
description: This pair of easy chairs was designed by Frits Schlegel in Denmark in the 1950s. The chairs are constructed in solid ash with backs and seats in woven rattan cane. The frames demonstrate Schlegel’s interest in clear construction and practical comfort. The gently curved backs and integrated armrests are formed from continuous sections of wood, providing support while reducing the number of individual components.The open cane backs contribute to a light visual expression. Slightly splayed legs connected by stretchers provide stability without adding unnecessary mass. Frits Schlegel was a Danish architect and designer associated with functionalism. His work emphasised durability and a rational use of materials rather than decorative effect. These easy chairs are representative of his approach and his contribution to mid-century Danish furniture design.

name: A pair of armchairs designed by Ivar Callmander
description: Designed by Swedish architect and designer Ivar Callmander in the 1920s, this rare pair of armchairs was commissioned as part of the interior furnishings for the iconic Kungstornen (King's Towers) in Stockholm. Callmander was responsible for the design of the southern tower, while the northern tower was designed by architect Sven Wallander. Completed in the mid-1920s, the twin towers are widely recognized as Europe's first modern skyscrapers, marking a significant milestone in Scandinavian architecture. The chairs perfectly reflect the progressive spirit of the project, combining natural woven wicker with slender blackened steel frames in a design that is both refined and forward-looking. Their elegant crescent-shaped backrests flow seamlessly into tapered armrests, while the handwoven seats showcase exceptional craftsmanship and warmth. The lightweight steel structure lends the chairs an airy architectural quality, emphasizing simplicity, comfort, and structural clarity. Commissioned specifically for one of Sweden's most important architectural landmarks, these armchairs are not only remarkable examples of early Scandinavian modern design but also rare historical pieces that embody the close relationship between architecture, interior design, and craftsmanship during the formative years of modernism.

name: Easy chair 'Star', designed by Mats Theselius for Källemo,
description: “Star” is an armchair conceived by Swedish designer Mats Theselius in collaboration with the manufacturer Källemo. Executed circa 2009, this limited‑edition piece (of a run of 360) blends sculptural presence with refined materiality. The chair features a slim tubular chrome frame, a generously proportioned seat and back upholstered in leather, and distinctive outer panelling of pearlescent synthetic material with a subtle mother‑of‑pearl finish. The form presents a softly curved backrest enveloping the sitter, contrasting with the crisp geometry of the structural frame. While firmly rooted in contemporary craftsmanship, the material references and details (such as riveted edges) recall industrial aesthetic cues—marking it as a thoughtful intersection of function and design expression. The Star chair is part of a numbered edition of 360. Its structure combines a tubular steel frame with a moulded shell in synthetic material and leather upholstery. The outer panels feature a pearlescent finish, fastened with exposed rivets along the edges. Materials should be evaluated for signs of surface wear, patina to the chrome, and the condition of upholstery and panel joints, which may vary depending on use and handling over time. Limited Edition: 248 / 360.

name: Armchair designed by Frits Henningsen
description: This armchair is the work of Danish designer and cabinetmaker Frits Henningsen, who was active in the first half of the 20th century and is known for producing his furniture entirely within his own Copenhagen workshop. Rather than relying on external manufacturers, he oversaw each stage of construction himself, from joinery to final finishing. This approach limited the number of pieces that could be produced but allowed for consistent control over materials, proportions, and surface treatment. At a time when industrial methods were becoming more common, Henningsen continued to work within a craft-based tradition and maintained construction methods rooted in cabinetmaking practice. The chair is built on a solid wood frame with a stained finish and connected by stretcher bars between the legs. The upholstery covers both seat and back, with the arms forming a continuous upholstered shell that curves inward. The backrest features evenly spaced button tufting, and the edges are finished with contrasting piping. Frits focus on rounded forms reflected his view that furniture should follow the body’s natural posture and be a comfortable sitting experience.

name: A pair of armchairs designed by Frits Henningsen
description: These exceptional armchairs are built on solid wood frames with mahogany-stained beech legs joined by stretcher bars. The upholstered seat, arms, and back form a continuous shell with a gently angled back and discreet button tufting. Piping follows the curved edges, and the exposed underframe reflects traditional joinery. At a time when many designers were moving toward stricter forms, Henningsen instead developed chairs with rounded, continuous profiles. His interest in historical furniture, including Rococo, French Empire, and English seventeenth-century pieces encountered during his travels, informed his preference for softer outlines and enclosed seating rather than exposed frames and sharp angles. Frits Henningsen (1889–1965) was a renowned Danish furniture designer and cabinetmaker, celebrated for his exceptional craftsmanship and dedication to traditional woodworking techniques. Unlike many of his contemporaries, Henningsen insisted on producing his designs exclusively in his own workshop, ensuring meticulous attention to detail and quality in every piece.

name: Easy chair 'Peacock' model JH521 designed by Hans J Wegner for Johannes Hansen
description: Hans J. Wegner's 1947 Peacock Chair (model PP550) exemplifies the fusion of traditional craftsmanship with modernist design principles. Drawing inspiration from the classic English Windsor chair, Wegner reinterpreted its form to create a piece that is both sculptural and functional.​ The chair's distinctive fan-like backrest, featuring flattened spindles, was likened to a peacock's tail by fellow designer Finn Juhl, giving the chair its enduring nickname. ​ Hans J. Wegner (1914–2007) was one of the most influential Danish furniture designers of the 20th century and a central figure in the Danish Modern movement. Often referred to as the Master of the Chair , he designed over 500 chairs in his lifetime, many of which have become icons of modern design such as the Peacock Chair.

name: Armchair designed by Hans Frost Nielsen
description: This armchair was designed in 1974 by the Danish craftsman Hans Frost Nielsen. Nielsen is best known for his long career in the drawing room of the cabinetmaking workshop PP Møbler, where he contributed to the technical development and production of high-quality furniture. In addition to this work, he became widely recognized for the miniature chairs he produced independently, demonstrating exceptional precision and craftsmanship. This armchair is a rare example of a full-scale furniture design produced under his own name. The chair is constructed with a solid beech frame featuring a distinct, angular profile. It has a low, reclined silhouette with armrests integrated into the frame. The seat and high backrest are formed from a single piece of heavy canvas stretched across the structure. The perimeter of the canvas is reinforced with stitched leather piping, adding strength and durability. Designed for lounge use, the chair has a low seat height and a reclined backrest. Its construction reflects the standards of Danish cabinetmaking, with an emphasis on structure, materials, and long-term use rather than ornamentation.

name: Pair of armchairs
description: This pair of armchairs was produced in Sweden in the 1930s and exemplifies the restrained furniture design that characterised the transitional period between Nordic Art Deco and early functionalism. The chairs are constructed with solid wooden frames finished in black lacquer. Their proportions are compact, with slightly reclined backs and rounded seat cushions. The seats and backs are upholstered in a light, neutral textile, creating a clear contrast with the dark frames and emphasising the structural outline. The backs are subtly tapered, and the framing elements are clearly articulated. Decorative details are limited, with emphasis placed on form, material contrast, and construction. Although unsigned, the chairs are representative of Swedish workshop production of the period that balanced craftsmanship, functionality, and understated elegance.

name: Easy chair
Folding stool 'Guldhøj’ designed by Poul Hundevad
description: This stool’s design was inspired by a fascinating piece of Danish history. In 1891, a team of archaeologists led by Vilhelm Boye excavated the Guldhøj burial mound in southern Jutland; a burial site dating back to around 1400 BCE. The dig unearthed a rare glimpse into the ancient craftsmanship practices of the Nordic Bronze Age as well as an incredibly rare and well-preserved stool. The unearthed stool was simple yet elegantly crafted as well as compact and lightweight. When Poul Hundevad designed his ‘Guldhøj’ folding stool in the 1960s, he drew direct inspiration from the original Bronze Age design. Hundevad modernised the stool, using rosewood and leather, materials prized for their beauty and durability, while maintaining the spirit of simplicity and functionality inherent in the ancient piece. The rosewood frame of Hundevad’s stool exhibits an exceptional depth of colour and stirking grain while the leather seat is carefully hand-stitched. In designing the ‘Guldhøj’ stool, Hundevad paid homage to Denmark's cultural heritage and demonstrated how timeless design principles could bridge millennia.

name: Rocking chair designed by Åke Axelsson, Sweden
description: Crafted from solid mahogany, with a seat and backrest of Swedish leather, it is a refined example of Scandinavian modernist design, seamlessly blending functionality, craftsmanship, and natural materials. Åke Axelsson (1932-2026) is one of Sweden’s most esteemed furniture designers and interior architects, with a career spanning over six decades. Axelsson’s work embodies the essence of Swedish modernism while maintaining a timeless appeal. Axelsson's approach prioritises functionality, simplicity, and sustainability. He often works with natural materials such as solid wood, embracing their qualities to create pieces that are durable, ergonomic, and aesthetically understated. His designs are rooted in the idea that furniture should serve people’s needs while ageing gracefully over time.

name: Easy chair designed by Hans Asplund for Nordiska Kompaniet, Sweden
description: This rare easy chair, designed by Hans Asplund for Nordiska Kompaniet in 1955, exemplifies Swedish mid-century modern design. Custom-made for the beauty salon at NK’s flagship department store in Stockholm, only six chairs were made and never offered for retail sale. Asplund’s collaboration with NK often involved site-specific furniture, tailored to complement the interiors of the store or other commissioned spaces. This particular chair highlights Asplund’s focus on functionality and elegance, featuring the walnut frame with elegant, flowing curves that define its sophisticated design paired with cognac leather upholstery. Hans Asplund (1921–1994) was a prominent Swedish architect and designer, belonging to the renowned Asplund family of architects, which included his father, Gunnar Asplund, one of Sweden’s most celebrated architectural figures. Hans Asplund is best known for his contributions to Swedish modernism, blending functionality with elegance in both architecture and furniture design.

name: A set of four chair model 'Corall' designed by Axel Einar Hjorth for Nordiska Kompaniet, Sweden
description: This set of four ‘Corall’ chairs, designed by Axel Einar Hjorth for Nordiska Kompaniet in 1937, reflects the practicality and simplicity characteristic of Swedish design during this period. Created for summer houses and cabins, the Corall series was designed to suit homes often located in natural or coastal environments. The name "Corall" likely references these settings, as Hjorth sought to create furniture that blended seamlessly with its surroundings. The use of birch and rattan highlights the focus on durability and natural materials. By 1937, Hjorth was nearing the end of his tenure at Nordiska Kompaniet, leaving the following year. During this time, his work began to prioritise accessibility and functionality, moving away from the Art Deco influences seen earlier in his career. The Corall series represents this shift toward a more restrained style, aligning with the principles of Swedish Modernism. Axel Einar Hjorth (1888–1959) was a prominent Swedish furniture designer known for blending modernist and traditional influences. From 1927 to 1938, he served as the chief designer at Nordiska Kompaniet (NK), where he created both luxurious Art Deco-inspired pieces and more rustic designs like his cabin furniture collections. Hjorth's career bridged high-end exclusivity and practical, nature-inspired design, leaving a lasting impact on Scandinavian furniture.

name: Easy chair designed by Otto Schulz for Boet, Sweden, 1940s
description: This vintage armchair is a refined example of Otto Schulz’s distinctive contribution to Swedish design. Inspired by the classical Greek klismos chair as well as his own well-known “Sulla” model, Schulz developed a broad, sculptural seat with a softly curved backrest that embraces the sitter. Rather than relying on a loose cushion, the chair features a deeply formed, integrated seat, giving the design a clear and modern outline that distinguishes it among vintage seating. Otto Schulz, founder of the influential firm and design magazine Boet , played a significant role in shaping Nordic interior culture during the early twentieth century. Today, this rare easy chair is appreciated as part of the wider Scandinavian modern tradition, standing comfortably alongside the most sought-after pieces of Danish and Swedish vintage furniture.

name: Stool
Set of four dining chairs model 78 designed by Niels O. Möller for J. L. Möller,
description: This set of four dining chairs, model 78, was designed by Niels O. Møller in 1962 and produced by J. L. Møllers Møbelfabrik. Crafted in richly grained rosewood with handwoven seats, the chairs exemplify the refined craftsmanship and sculptural lightness associated with Danish modern furniture. The design is distinguished by its gently curved backrest and the subtle, horn-like endings of the back of the seat. Niels Otto Møller (1920–1982) was one of Denmark’s most respected furniture designers and cabinetmakers. After training as a cabinetmaker, he founded J. L. Møllers Møbelfabrik in 1944, where his designs were produced with an uncompromising focus on craftsmanship and materials. His chairs, known for their elegant proportions and meticulous construction, remain among the most celebrated examples of Danish modern design.

name: Set of fourteen dining chairs designed by Niels O Møller for JL Møller
description: The twelve dining chairs are model 65, originally designed in 1962. The two armchairs are model 80, originally designed in 1968. All fourteen chairs were manufactured in the 1970s.

name: 'The Propeller Stool' designed by Kaare Klint for Rud. Rasmussen
Daybed designed by Erik Riisager Hansen for Haslev, Denmark.
description: This daybed, designed by Erik Riisager and produced by Haslev in the 1950s, reflects the restrained and functional approach characteristic of Danish furniture from the period. The piece is defined by its elongated, slightly tapered form and subtly raised ends, which provide both visual balance and practical support. The frame is executed in rosewood, a material widely used in higher-quality Danish production at the time for its durability and distinctive grain. Slender, gently angled legs emphasise lightness and stability. The linen upholstery is simple and continuous, following the outline of the structure without interruption. A central support beneath the seat ensures structural integrity across its length. Daybeds were a common feature in Scandinavian interiors, used as both seating and a place to rest, reflecting a practical and flexible approach to domestic space. The slightly upturned ends serve as understated head and foot rests, reinforcing the functional logic of the design. Produced by Haslev Møbelsnedkeri, the piece demonstrates a consistent focus on proportion, craftsmanship, and usability.

name: Stool 'The Unrockable' designed by Hans Sandgren Jakobsen for Werner
description: This stool, titled Unrockable , was designed by Hans Sandgren Jakobsen. The piece is constructed from thirty-five turned wooden staves, each topped with a rounded knob and inserted into a rectangular base. Together they form a gently concave seating surface, creating a stable stool. The design draws visual inspiration from organic and everyday forms, including the delicate structure of a flower’s stamen and the shape of a midwife’s stethoscope. Jakobsen conceived the object as both a useful piece of furniture and a visual statement, offering a light-hearted contrast to more rigid or conventional design. As part of the same design exploration, Jakobsen also developed a related piece titled Rockable . This version uses thirty-seven staves set into a circular base to form a convex seat that allows the stool to rock gently in response to the sitter’s movement. Hans Sandgren Jakobsen (b. 1963) was born in Copenhagen and trained at the Danish Design School. Working as both a designer and craftsman, he approaches design as a discipline grounded in usability rather than pure artistic expression. His work often combines clear, minimal forms with thoughtful construction and his travels abroad have been an ongoing source of inspiration for his designs. Stamped.

name: Pair of chairs designed by Erik Chambert
Sofa 'Utö' designed by Axel Einar Hjorth for Nordiska Kompaniet
description: From 1927 to 1938, Axel-Einar Hjorth was the chief architect and designer at the department store Nordiska Kompaniet in Stockholm—which was known as one of the most important producers of modernist furniture in Sweden. During this time, Hjorth designed both public and private interiors, and worked with international clients including Iranian royalty. His first project for NK was a stand for the World Fair in Barcelona in 1929, during which he exhibited the Louis Cabinet and Caesar Cabinet. In the 1930s, Hjorth took a different direction, designing far less ornamental furniture out of pine meant for serial production which mixed handicraft with international modernism. Hjorth's designs - whether from the luxuriousness of neo-classicism to the severity of functionalism - are sharply distinct in style, materials, and character. Unlike many of his contemporaries however, he did not conform to the socially oriented ideas produced by Svensk Form. He often incorporated playful ornamentation from different historical periods from which he was inspired, such as French Art Deco, using mixed exotic woods, bright colours, and textiles.

name: Pair of armchairs ‘Eva’ designed by Bruno Mathsson for Karl Mathsson
description: With its characteristically curved legs and armrests, this iconic chair model "Eva" exemplifies Swedish functionalism. The comfortable seat is composed of beautifully patinated plaited leather straps in cognac — "Eva" in leather was only introduced in the 1960s. While the design aesthetic is delicate, both chairs are very well-made and sturdy because of the strong plywood. Bruno Mathsson’s love for nature pervades all his designs — he frequently slept outside in the forest or his garden on a specially designed foldable bed. His furniture shapes, particularly the legs, bring bull's horns or insects to mind. Mathsson was one of the most important Swedish designers of the 20th century. He was a contemporary of Alvar Aalto and Marcel Breuer, all of whom had already experimented with bent plywood during the 1930s. Karl Mathsson, Bruno Mathsson's father, was the fifth generation in a family of master cabinet makers. He owned a furniture manufacturing company that produced the earlier pieces; later, they founded "Mathsson International". The stamp indicates the manufacturing date and, sometimes, the design date. Bruno Mathsson often gave his furniture Swedish woman's names like "Eva", "Pernilla", or "Annika". Stamped.

name: A pair of armchairs and sofa for Paul Boman
Rocking stool 'Rockable' designed by Hans Sandgren Jakobsen for Orebo
description: 'Rockable' designed by Hans Sandgren Jakobsen in 1999 for Orebo, explores the relationship between movement, structure and form. The stool is constructed from thirty-seven turned wooden rods inserted into a circular base, each topped with a softly rounded knob. Together they create a gently convex seating surface that allows the stool to rock subtly in response to the sitter’s weight. The visual character of the piece draws inspiration from organic forms such as the stamen of a flower, as well as from a midwife’s stethoscope. While playful in appearance, the stool remains carefully engineered, balancing stability with controlled movement. Hans Sandgren Jakobsen (b. 1963) is a Danish designer trained at the Danish Design School in Copenhagen. Working at the intersection of craftsmanship and industrial design, he emphasises that design should be both functional and accessible rather than purely artistic. His work combines minimal forms with thoughtful construction, often drawing inspiration from his travels and observations of everyday life. Stamped.

name: Stool designed by Mogens Lassen for K. Thomsen
description: Made by cabinetmaker K.Thomsen. Stamped.

name: Lounge chair 'Pernilla 3' designed by Bruno Mathsson for Karl Mathsson
description: The lounge chair ‘Pernilla 3’ was designed in 1944 by Bruno Mathsson. The model was named after the journalist Pernilla Thunberger who visited Bruno Mathsson for an interview earlier that same year. This ‘Pernilla’ was a special commission from 1946/ 1947 by a tall customer who wanted a longer version. While the design aesthetic is delicate, the chair is very well-made and sturdy because of the strong laminated birch. With its characteristically ergonomic design, curved legs and armrests, this iconic chair model ‘Pernilla 3’ exemplifies Swedish functionalism. It is among the most comfortable of seats imaginable. The seat is composed of red, original paper webbing — paper was used for production during and after the years of World War II because all the hemp webbing went to the military. Bruno Mathsson (1907 - 1988), a prominent figure in Scandinavian furniture design, is revered for his distinctive style characterised by a harmonious fusion of form and function. Mathsson’s love for nature pervades all his designs — he frequently slept outside in the forest or his garden on a specially designed foldable bed. His furniture shapes, particularly the legs, bring bull's horns or insects to mind. Mathsson was one of the most important Swedish designers of the 20th century. He was a contemporary of Alvar Aalto and Marcel Breuer, all of whom had already experimented with bent plywood during the 1930s. Karl Mathsson, Bruno Mathsson's father, was the fifth generation in a family of master cabinet makers. He owned a furniture manufacturing company that produced the earlier pieces; later, they founded "Mathsson International". The stamp indicates the manufacturing date and, sometimes, the design date. Bruno Mathsson often gave his furniture Swedish woman's names like "Eva", "Pernilla", or "Annika". Stamped.

name: Chaise longue model PK 24 designed by Poul Kjærholm for E. Kold Christensen
description: Danish furniture designer Poul Kjærholm (1929–1980) was renowned for his innovative use of steel as a primary material, which he often paired with natural elements such as leather, wood, marble and cane. The PK24, referred to as the "hammock chair" due to its flowing, organic shape exemplifies Kjærholm’s design philosophy. Kjærholm’s use of cane and stainless steel makes it a sustainable design—decades ahead of today's emphasis on sustainability in design. The PK24 was produced by E. Kold Christensen, Kjærholm's primary manufacturer and exclusive producer during his lifetime. Christensen’s workshop specialised in the precision metalwork that Kjærholm’s designs demanded. The curvature of the stainless-steel frame on the PK24 required advanced metalworking techniques, as the material needed to be bent and polished without compromising its structural integrity. The PK24 is considered a masterpiece of 20th-century design and is part of the permanent collection at the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) in New York. Today, Fritz Hansen owns the rights to Kjærholm’s designs and continues to produce the PK24. However, the original PK24 chairs produced by E. Kold Christensen are particularly celebrated due to their rarity and because of close relationship between Kjaerholm and Christensen.

name: 'The Propeller Stool' model 8783 designed by Kaare Klint for Rud. Rasmussens Cabinetmakers
description: Kaare Klint was the father of Scandinavian modernism and is responsible for bringing Danish design to the centre stage. History has rarely seen such an impact left on the world of design by just one person, as Kaare Klint created a design language that would be spoken by designers for decades to come. The Danish golden age and Scandinavian modernism are periods that made Kaare Klint’s name synonymous with icon. Kaare Klint’s appreciation for clean lines, simple ornamentation and an understanding of the human body translated into a design philosophy that has truly influenced the designs of today. Kaare Klint crafted pieces that embodied a perfect balance of form and function. This balance was achieved from his education as an apprentice in his father’s architectural practice. This is where he was educated in classic realism and ergonomics, this allowed him to understand the proportions and requirements of furniture. Kaare Klint’s training focused a great deal on classical design on a global scale. Egyptian neoclassical design elements run through the veins of pieces. The pieces Kaare Klint crafted encapsulate technical perfection, masked by a minimalist aesthetic. The joinery flawlessly fits together, questioning whether the pieces were crafted from a single block of wood. Kaare Klint’s legacy was imbued in the physical, his architectural and furniture masterpieces and the philosophical, as a lecturer Kaare Klint passed on his knowledge to students that would continue to inspire pieces based on his design philosophy. Signed.

name: Stool designed by Ejner Larsen and Aksel Bender Madsen for Willy Beck
Chaise longue for Louis G Thiersen
description: This chaise longue reflects a restrained neoclassical influence within early 20th-century Danish furniture design. The elongated form is defined by a single scrolled backrest and a continuous upholstered seat, allowing for a reclining position while maintaining a compact footprint. The frame is executed in lacquered wood with gilded details, creating a clear contrast between the dark structure and the decorative elements. A continuous Greek key frieze runs along the apron, reinforcing the classical reference while remaining integrated into the overall construction. The legs are slightly splayed and carved with modest shaping, providing stability and visual balance. The upholstery is smooth and unbuttoned, emphasising the clarity of the silhouette and the overall proportion of the piece. The scroll at the backrest introduces a sculptural accent without interrupting the linear composition. Produced in 1928, the chaise longue illustrates a transitional moment in Danish design, where historicist ornament and classical motifs coexist with a growing emphasis on simplified forms and functional clarity. Unique

name: Armchair
Set of six chairs model 2025 designed by Josef Frank for Svenskt Tenn
description: This set of six dining chairs, model 2025, was designed by Josef Frank and produced by Svenskt Tenn. The slender construction reflects Frank’s belief that a dining chair should be light and easy to move — ideally so light that it could be lifted with a single finger. Originally conceived in 1925 for his Viennese firm Haus & Garten, the design balances graceful proportions with everyday practicality. The chairs feature a refined frame in black lacquered wood with vertical back spindles in a contrasting light tone, a combination that creates subtle visual tension within the structure. Frank frequently combined different woods and materials in his furniture to achieve this dynamic effect. The seats are upholstered in Svenskt Tenn’s Terrazzo textile, a lively pattern designed by Frank in 1944 as part of a group of “birthday textiles” created to celebrate Estrid Ericson’s fiftieth birthday. Josef Frank (1885–1967) was an Austrian-born architect, designer, and artist who later became a Swedish citizen. After relocating to Sweden in the 1930s, he began a long collaboration with Estrid Ericson and her company Svenskt Tenn. There he developed a distinctive design language that combined Viennese elegance with the functional ideals of Scandinavian modernism. His furniture, textiles, and interiors remain among the most celebrated expressions of twentieth-century Swedish design. Marked.

name: Easy chair designed by Alvar Andersson for Ferdinand Lundquist & Co
description: This easy chair designed by Alvar Andersson in the 1940s embodies the principles of Swedish Modern design, a style characterised by organic forms and the thoughtful use of natural materials. Crafted in elm, the chair features a sculptural frame with gently angled legs and armrests, creating a balanced and inviting silhouette. The upholstered seat and backrest provide generous comfort, while the softly curved, wing-like back gives the piece a distinctive character. The chair was produced by Ferdinand Lundquist & Co. in Gothenburg, a prestigious department store known for commissioning high-quality furniture for its clientele. These pieces were often designed specifically for the store’s interiors and customers. Alvar Andersson was an important contributor to Swedish furniture design during the mid-twentieth century. Early in his career he worked for Hyresgästernas Möbelaffär, where he developed flexible furniture solutions for modern homes. In the early 1940s he joined the design office of Ferdinand Lundquist & Co., and later became head of the drawing office at AB Svenska Kontorsmöbelindustrier (Aski), continuing to shape Swedish furniture design through both residential and office furnishings. Marked.

name: Pair of dining chairs designed by Axel Einar Hjorth for Nordiska Kompaniet
description: This pair of dining chairs, designed by Axel Einar Hjorth in 1934 for Nordiska Kompaniet, reflects the refined elegance associated with Swedish Art Deco design. The tall, oval-shaped backrests create a striking vertical silhouette, balanced by a compact upholstered seat and gently tapered legs. The frames are veneered in Macassar ebony, a richly figured wood prized for its dramatic linear grain. Historical records indicate that this model was originally used in the restaurant of Sportpalatset at S:t Eriksbron in Stockholm. Axel Einar Hjorth (1888–1959) was one of Sweden’s most influential furniture designers of the early twentieth century. After moving to Stockholm in the early 1900s, he worked with several prominent manufacturers before becoming chief architect at Nordiska Kompaniet from 1927 to 1938. Hjorth’s work is distinguished by its ability to combine modernist ideas with traditional craftsmanship and his designs played an important role in establishing Swedish furniture on the international stage. Stamped.

name: Sofa designed by Axel Einar Hjorth for Nordiska Kompaniet
description: This corner sofa designed by Axel Einar Hjorth in the 1930s for Nordiska Kompaniet reflects the refined elegance of Swedish furniture from the transitional period between Swedish Grace and early functionalism. Upholstered in velvet, the sofa is composed of two gently angled sections that form a welcoming corner arrangement. The sofa rests on a discreet blackened wooden plinth rather than visible legs, giving the piece a grounded architectural presence. This approach was characteristic of Hjorth’s more exclusive interior commissions, where furniture was conceived as part of a cohesive spatial design. Historical sources link this model to a private commission for Fredrik Anderzon, manager of the Nässjö Bryggeri, who commissioned a modernist summer house in 1936. Its rounded forms and monumental simplicity share a visual relationship with Hjorth’s celebrated “Borgen” series, known for similarly sculptural seating designs. Axel Einar Hjorth (1888–1959) was one of Sweden’s most influential furniture designers of the early twentieth century. After moving to Stockholm in the early 1900s, he worked with several leading manufacturers before becoming chief architect at Nordiska Kompaniet from 1927 to 1938. Hjorth’s work is recognised for its ability to unite modernist ideas with traditional craftsmanship, helping to establish Swedish furniture design on the international stage.

name: Stool designed by Ingvar Kamprad for Habitat
Set of six dining chairs 'Poem' designed by Erik Chambert
description: This extraordinarily light and delicate high-backed chair design called “the Poem Chair” is comfortable and very strong. Interestingly, the cane is pierced on different levels of the seat instead of going all around the frame to achieve a decorative effect. The chair was initially available in natural birch or this elegant, very light grey. The “Poem Chair” by Erik Chambert is often falsely regarded as influenced by Gio Ponti’s “Superleggera” when, in fact, it predates Ponti’s chair by at least a year. Erik Chambert studied design in the late 1920s and presented his furniture for the first time at the Stockholm Exhibition in 1930. He and his brother took over the family furniture-making business from their father. Chambert is responsible for many pieces now considered Swedish design classics, one of the most famous being this “Poem Chair,” designed in 1953.

name: Easy chair designed by Otto Schulz, for Boet
description: This Schulz model is one of the designer’s rarest and finest chairs. It has been newly reupholstered in the most luxurious Boucle fabric by one of Sweden’s best reupholsters. Otto Schulz was one of the most prominent furniture designers of his time; he founded the Swedish company Boet and an eponymous magazine that became an extremely influential design publication during the 1930s and 40s. This chair is based on the “Sulla chair” and the Greek klismos chairs. Schulz made several versions; the most refined is this one without an added loose seat cushion. Instead, he created one deep seat to perfect his sense of modern elegance.

name: Stool designed by Calle Warfvinge
description: This unique Swedish stool by Calle Warfvinge is a quiet masterclass in Scandinavian design and craftsmanship. Each element of the construction is carefully selected ash wood, chosen for its grain and tone to create a subtle decorative interplay across the piece. The angled legs intersect and overlap in an almost architectural way, joined with visible through tenons that form a refined pattern on the seat surface and celebrate the honesty of the construction. Born and based in Skåne, in the south of Sweden, Warfvinge brings his background as a boat builder to his furniture, translating maritime precision into finely detailed, handcrafted furniture. He works exclusively with high-quality timber sourced from the forests surrounding his home, allowing the material to guide both form and proportion. The result is a contemporary piece of Swedish design that feels both robust and sculptural, well suited to collectors looking for distinctive, small-scale Scandinavian furniture.

name: Set of twelve dining chairs ‘Darby’ designed by Torbjörn Afdal for Bruksbo
description: This dining chair model 'Darby' is simple yet elegant with a sophisticated high backrest and small carved details at the top of the legs. The generous, padded back has a slight curve to support the lumbar region of the spine. The chair is extremely comfortable and has elegant side stretchers that add extra stability. The deep colouring of the rosewood frame appears particularly striking when combined with black leather upholstery. The design shows slightly elongated front legs, which is echoed in the proportions of the back. The front leg protrusions make such high-quality leather upholstery incredibly difficult to achieve. All chairs are in excellent condition and become an appealing set combined with the matching 'Darby' dining table . Torbjörn Afdal was one of Norway's most prolific designers during the 1950s and 60s. He was the leading designer at the internationally acclaimed company Bruksbo, where he realised several iconic designs in rosewood.

name: Sofa ‘Royal’ designed by Werner West for Oy Stockmann AB
description: The “Royal” sofa by Werner West is wonderfully comfortable and elegant with its high, enveloping backrest and integrated arms. The cut-out fronts and fine Boucle upholstery give the sizeable piece its modern aesthetic, while the tall back legs offer strong support by kicking out for extra balance. Werner West designed his celebrated “Hugging Chair” in the 1930s and is known today as one of Finland’s most important 20th-century seating designers.

name: Set of six dining chairs model 526 designed by Josef Frank for Svenskt Tenn
description: The combination of mahogany and rattan in Josef Frank’s chair model 526 reflects a colonial-style influence, making it a particularly distinctive design. It is rare to find a complete set of these chairs, adding to their uniqueness. The seat is upholstered in Frank’s vibrant Anakreon textile, inspired by a 3,500-year-old fresco from a Cretan palace. Named after the Greek poet Anacreon, known for his verses on love and wine, the pattern embodies Frank’s ability to blend historical references with bold, modern expression. Marked Bodafors SMF

name: 'Clam' Chair designed by Arnold Madsen for Madsen & Schubell
description: The ‘Clam’, upholstered in soft sheepskin, is among the most comfortable chairs imaginable – it is both a recognisable and desirable Scandinavian design. As the name indicates, the design resembles the sea creature with a shell in two parts. In 1944, Arnold Madsen designed the ‘Clam’ chair in his small basement workshop in Gothersgade, Copenhagen. The design has a fascinating history as it has been attributed to several designers, frequently to the Danish architect Phillip Arctander. But recent research revealed that the “Clam” is in fact the model that started the story of Madsen & Schubell.

name: Pair of easy chairs
Stool 'Futura' by David Rosen for Nordiska Kompaniet
description: Designed by David Rosén for Nordiska Kompaniet (NK) in 1951, the Futura stool is a quintessential example of Swedish mid-century modern design. Although relatively little is known about Rosén’s life, his work for NK throughout the 1950s established him as one of the company's most accomplished designers. Developed as part of the celebrated Futura series, introduced in 1949, this folding stool reflects Rosén’s commitment to combining refined craftsmanship with practical innovation. Its elegant X-frame, crafted in warm-toned wood, supports a suspended leather seat that offers both comfort and remarkable visual lightness. The subtle curves of the frame, together with the exposed brass fittings, demonstrate the restrained sophistication that defines Scandinavian modernism. Designed to fold effortlessly, the stool answers the post-war demand for functional, adaptable furniture while maintaining an unmistakable sense of elegance. Rosén frequently worked with carefully selected woods, including pine, beech, teak, and mahogany, and collaborated with leading designers such as Stig Lindberg during his years at NK. Today, the Futura stool remains an enduring icon of Scandinavian design, admired for its timeless aesthetic, ingenious construction, and exceptional craftsmanship Marked.

name: Sofa designed by N.D. Hansen and Flemming Johansen for cabinetmaker Ove Lander
description: This very rare three-seater sofa was first exhibited at the 1936 Copenhagen Cabinetmakers’ Guild Exhibition, an annual furniture exhibition and competition held from 1927 to 1966. It was the main platform for design in Scandinavia during these years, so the designers and cabinetmakers presented only their very best work. The sofa was made by the master cabinetmaker Ole Lander and was produced in very small numbers, if at all. The sofa is comfortable and elegant but also remarkably practical. The upholstery stands out because of the ingenious way the front sections of the armrests have been left bare — a very suitable way of protecting the upholstery in those places that are commonly first to suffer from everyday wear. By allowing the polished Cuban mahogany to protrude, a sense of lightness is added to the overall design. The sofa has been newly upholstered in a linen blend material and contrasting leather piping.

name: Armchair designed by Hans J. Wegner for Johannes Hansen
description: Designed around 1959, this armchair is a particularly clear example of Hans J. Wegner’s exploration of the relationship between solid wood structures and suspended textile elements. Made of oak, it features a distinctly architectural frame: slightly splayed uprights, subtly curved lower rails, and softly shaped armrests designed to follow the natural movement of the arm. The seat and back are formed of tensioned canvas, suspended within the wooden structure and held in place by cylindrical rods with discreet yet visible metal fittings. This suspended construction replaces upholstery and gives the chair a marked visual lightness, while providing comfort through the flexibility and tension of the material. The back is articulated by a geometric stitched pattern that is both functional and graphic, reinforcing the canvas without disrupting the overall restraint of the design. The Johannes Hansen / Copenhagen / Denmark stamp, together with the HH monogram, confirms workshop production. This armchair reflects the maturity of Wegner’s work in the late 1950s, where structural clarity, economy of means, and carefully judged proportions come together in a form that is both rigorous and warm. Hans J. Wegner is widely regarded as the father of Danish design and is renowned for creating some of the most iconic chairs of the past hundred years. Considered the most influential figure within the Danish modern movement, Wegner produced more than 500 designs that combine beauty, functionality, and exceptional craftsmanship. He described his furniture as an effort to be “as simple and genuine as possible, to show what we could create with our hands, to make wood come alive, to give it spirit and vitality, and to make things so natural that they could only have been made by us.” Stamped.

name: Stool designed by Ingvar Hildingsson for I.H. Slöjd
description: This stool was designed by Ingvar Hildingsson and produced by his workshop I.H. Slöjd in Rockneby, Sweden during the 1970s. Crafted from solid birch, the piece is defined by its compact proportions and sculptural simplicity. A thick, circular seat rests on three gently tapered legs with rounded, club-like profiles, giving the stool a sturdy yet playful character. The design emphasises the natural qualities of the wood, allowing the distinct grain of the birch to become an integral part of the object’s visual expression. Its straightforward construction and balanced form make it versatile in use, functioning equally well as a stool or as a small side table. Ingvar Hildingsson was a Swedish designer and craftsman active during the mid to late twentieth century. Through his company I.H. Slöjd, he produced furniture that combined elements of traditional Swedish woodworking with the pared-back aesthetic of Scandinavian modern design. His work is characterised by solid construction, honest materials and a clear emphasis on craftsmanship. Marked.

name: Armchair 42 'Small Paimio' designed by Alvar Aalto
description: Armchair 42 – or “Small Paimio” – was designed by Alvar Aalto for the Paimio Sanatorium in 1931. The frame is made from laminated birch shaped to produce a cantilevered chair; the seat and back are created from one piece of form-pressed plywood. The fluidity of the design creates a soft, comfortable place to sit. The result is an armchair without straight lines, an armchair of exceptional aesthetic appeal. Since wood changes over time, the armrests are formed from a single piece that is then split in half, ensuring that as the chair ages, it remains perfectly balanced. This is considered one of Aalto’s masterpieces. Alvar Aalto was a Finnish architect and designer. His work includes architecture, furniture, lighting, and glassware, as well as sculptures and paintings. He never regarded himself as an artist, seeing painting and sculpture as "branches of the tree whose trunk is architecture." The pure Functionalist phase in Aalto’s work lasted for several years. It enabled him to make an international breakthrough, largely because of Paimio Sanatorium (1929-1933), an important Functionalist milestone. Aalto had adopted the principles of user-friendly, functional design in his architecture, and it was characteristic of Aalto to treat each building as a complete work of art – right down to the furniture and light fittings. The design of his furniture combined practicality and aesthetics with series production, encouraging a more beautiful everyday life in the home. Stamped.

name: Eight chairs 'Celestina' by Marco Zanuso for Zanotta
description: Set of eight ‘Celestina’ folding chairs, designed by Marco Zanuso for Zanotta in 1978. The design reinterprets the traditional folding chair within Zanotta’s late-1970s approach to redesigning familiar typologies. The original anonymous outdoor folding chair was found in a second-hand furniture shop; Aurelio Zanotta had also encountered the model on the Croisette in Cannes and subsequently asked Zanuso to reinterpret it. Zanuso retained the essential structure of the chair while refining its functionality and comfort. The frame is made of painted steel, while the seat and backrest consist of nylon slats covered in saddle leather and secured to the structure with copper nails. Lightweight and functional, the chair folds down to only a few centimetres for easy storage. ‘Celestina’ is held in the collections of the Design Museum, London, the Vitra Design Museum, Weil am Rhein, and the Fondazione Triennale Design Museum, Milan. Stamped.

name: Bench designed by Hans Wegner for Johannes Hansen
description: Reflecting Wegner’s characteristic design philosophy, this bench is a masterpiece of simplicity, functionality, and timeless beauty. The sturdy, tapered legs provide a strong foundation while maintaining a light visual presence. The proportions are perfectly balanced, creating a sense of stability without bulkiness. The rounded edges of the bench soften its angular form, demonstrating Wegner’s mastery of blending organic and geometric lines. This understated design is versatile, serving as a bench, a coffee table, or even a display piece. This particular piece, originating from a private Danish collection, is a testament to Wegner’s enduring influence on modern furniture design. Stamped.

name: Easy chairs designed by Bodil Kjaer for Harbo Sølvsten
description: "The chairs were designed for the modernist house "Doktorn 5" in the town Laholm, Sweden, in 1956, by architect Svend Bøgh-Andersen (1916-1984), who built and decorated it for him and his wife Hanne (1920-2015)" Four available. Sold individually.

name: Sofa 'Colonial' designed by Ole Wanscher for P Jeppesen
description: The sofa’s name is a reference to Ole Wanscher’s fascination with English furnishings from the 1700s. The sofa is remarkably light and was designed for production, with removable cushions. This piece was originally produced by Poul Jeppesen Møbelfabrik from 1949. Small and intricate details, such as the turned tops of the front legs and the inclusion of loops on the tops of the cushions, show that every detail was thought through during the design process.

name: The Bull chair model JH 518 designed by Hans Wegner for Johannes Hansen
description: The Bull Chair, model JH 518, designed by Hans J. Wegner for Johannes Hansen in 1961, is a striking example of Wegner’s sculptural approach to furniture design. This particular example, crafted in lacquered pine, stands out as an early production model, possibly even a prototype, making it a unique and significant piece. The chair is named for its distinctive backrest, which features broad, horn-like extensions that give it a bold and dynamic character. This bold form balances aesthetics and comfort, while the rest of the design showcases Wegner’s signature focus on simplicity and ergonomic functionality.

name: Set of four chairs 'Futurum' designed by Axel Einar Hjorth for Nordiska Kompaniet
description: From 1927 to 1938, Axel-Einar Hjorth was the chief architect and designer at the department store Nordiska Kompaniet in Stockholm—which was known as one of the most important producers of modernist furniture in Sweden. During this time, Hjorth designed both public and private interiors, and worked with international clients including Iranian royalty. His first project for NK was a stand for the World Fair in Barcelona in 1929, during which he exhibited the Louis Cabinet and Caesar Cabinet. In the 1930s, Hjorth took a different direction, designing far less ornamental furniture out of pine meant for serial production which mixed handicraft with international modernism. Hjorth's designs - whether from the luxuriousness of neo-classicism to the severity of functionalism - are sharply distinct in style, materials, and character. Unlike many of his contemporaries however, he did not conform to the socially oriented ideas produced by Svensk Form. He often incorporated playful ornamentation from different historical periods from which he was inspired, such as French Art Deco, using mixed exotic woods, bright colours, and textiles.

name: Set of four 'Bull' armchairs model JH 518 designed by Hans Wegner for Johannes Hansen
description: This chair model was presented at the Copenhagen Cabinetmakers' Guild Exhibition in 1961. The curved backrest of Hans Wegner’s model JH 518 extends into armrests that resemble bull horns — hence the name ‘Bull’, further suggested by the slightly splayed, tapering legs. With its broad leather seat and considered support for the back and arms, the ‘Bull’ offers a well-balanced seating experience. The design is also marked by six contrasting tenons, which serve both a decorative and structural purpose. Hans Wegner (1914–2007) is among the most recognised Danish furniture designers and is often referred to as “the master of the chair”. He combined simplicity and function with refined form, leaving a significant mark on Scandinavian design history. Wegner was part of the generation responsible for what is now known as the Golden Age of modern Danish design. To realise many of his now well-known pieces, Wegner often collaborated with the cabinetmaker Johannes Hansen, whose initials are referenced in the model name JH 518.

name: Children's Rocking Chair designed by Carl Hörvik for Nordiska Kompaniet
Pair of armchairs model 3758 A designed by Kaare Klint for Rud. Rasmussen
description: Model designed in 1927 for the Danish Museum of Decorative Art, produced by Rud Rasmussen in the 1940's. Kaare Klint was the father of Scandinavian modernism and is responsible for bringing Danish design to the centre stage. History has rarely seen such an impact left on the world of design by just one person, as Kaare Klint created a design language that would be spoken by designers for decades to come. The Danish golden age and Scandinavian modernism are periods that made Kaare Klint’s name synonymous with icon. Kaare Klint’s appreciation for clean lines, simple ornamentation and an understanding of the human body translated into a design philosophy that has truly influenced the designs of today. Kaare Klint crafted pieces that embodied a perfect balance of form and function. This balance was achieved from his education as an apprentice in his father’s architectural practice. This is where he was educated in classic realism and ergonomics, this allowed him to understand the proportions and requirements of furniture. Kaare Klint’s training focused a great deal on classical design on a global scale. Egyptian neoclassical design elements run through the veins of pieces. The pieces Kaare Klint crafted encapsulate technical perfection, masked by a minimalist aesthetic. The joinery flawlessly fits together, questioning whether the pieces were crafted from a single block of wood. Kaare Klint’s legacy was imbued in the physical, his architectural and furniture masterpieces and the philosophical, as a lecturer Kaare Klint passed on his knowledge to students that would continue to inspire pieces based on his design philosophy. Marked.

name: Stool 'Sauna' designed by Bertel Gardberg for Villa Jouhki
description: Very rare, custom order apachi stool. Originally designed for Villa Jouhki.

name: Set of three chairs 'Typenko' designed by Axel Einar Hjorth for Nordiska Kompaniet,
description: From 1927 to 1938, Axel-Einar Hjorth was the chief architect and designer at the department store Nordiska Kompaniet in Stockholm—which was known as one of the most important producers of modernist furniture in Sweden. During this time, Hjorth designed both public and private interiors, and worked with international clients including Iranian royalty. His first project for NK was a stand for the World Fair in Barcelona in 1929, during which he exhibited the Louis Cabinet and Caesar Cabinet. In the 1930s, Hjorth took a different direction, designing far less ornamental furniture out of pine meant for serial production which mixed handicraft with international modernism. Hjorth's designs - whether from the luxuriousness of neo-classicism to the severity of functionalism - are sharply distinct in style, materials, and character. Unlike many of his contemporaries however, he did not conform to the socially oriented ideas produced by Svensk Form. He often incorporated playful ornamentation from different historical periods from which he was inspired, such as French Art Deco, using mixed exotic woods, bright colours, and textiles. Marked.

name: Pair of armchairs in the style of Jean Royère
Set of ten dining chairs designed by Aino Aalto for Artek
Stool / Bench
Folding stool designed by Jörgen Gammelgaard for Forum Design
Children’s chair 'Lilla M' designed by Caroline Schlyter
description: Lacquered plywood construction formed from a single continuous curve. Sculptural, flowing profile integrating seat, backrest and base, with a circular cut-out detail to the back. Designed in the 1990s, Lilla M reflects a renewed interest in bent and laminated wood techniques, allowing for more fluid and experimental forms. Its continuous silhouette recalls earlier Scandinavian organic modernism, while introducing a more playful character. Conceived for children, the chair combines compact proportions with a stable base, ensuring comfort and everyday use. Its sculptural quality also gives it a strong visual presence, functioning both as a practical object and a design statement. Signed.

name: Prototype wall bench and foot rest, designed by Gunnar Aagaard Andersen for PP Möbler
description: This prototype wall bench and accompanying footrest were designed by Gunnar Aagaard Andersen for PP Møbler in Denmark during the 1980s. The piece combines a solid wooden base with a woven seating surface composed of wide leather straps, fixed with visible rivets along the sides. The construction emphasises both structure and flexibility, allowing the seat to adapt slightly to the body while maintaining a clear, geometric form. The bench is conceived for wall mounting, with its gently curved profile suggesting an ergonomic consideration unusual for such a compact format. The separate footrest, executed in matching wood, extends its functional use and reinforces the intended seated posture. Aagaard Andersen, known for his work across painting, sculpture and design, often explored modularity and material contrast. This prototype reflects that approach through the combination of rigid wood elements and the softer, interlaced leather surface. The visible joinery and fastening details underline the construction rather than concealing it. As a prototype, the piece also documents a stage in development, offering insight into experimentation within Danish furniture design during the late twentieth century.

name: Pair of stools
description: Beech wood frames raised on four tapered legs. Gently curved, saddle-shaped seats offering good comfort. Original patterned wool upholstery. The design is defined by its lightness and balanced proportions, with a clear functional approach. The slightly angled legs and sculpted seats add a subtle dynamism while maintaining the restrained character typical of Danish mid-century furniture.
